p.b: After a month of scorching heat, it finally rained today. Since morning, dark clouds had gathered in the sky. When the rain began at noon, a sweet smell rose from the wet earth. The children of our lane floated paper boats on the little streams running beside the road. Radha's boat floated the longest because she had made it from thick paper. The happiest person was our farmer uncle. He said the first rain of Sawan is like a blessing for his paddy fields. When the rain stopped, a rainbow of seven colours spread across the sky.

When the queen of morning wakes, light spills everywhere,

Little sparrows softly say, 'May we find our share.'

Pecking grains and hopping on, they build their nests in thorn,

Mothers feed the little chicks and sing a tune at morn.

The pond of Harita village was once alive with water birds. Gradually, people began throwing garbage into it. The water turned dirty, fish began to die, and the elderly who spent their evenings on its banks stopped coming. Then the village children, along with their teacher, formed a 'Save the Pond Team'. Every Sunday they collected litter from the banks with brooms, baskets and gloves. Slowly, the adults of the village joined them. In three months, the water became so clean that pairs of sarus cranes returned. The head of the village declared that twice a year the whole village would care for the pond together. Small hands had changed the habits of an entire village.

Plant a tree and save a breath, let the oxygen grow,

Shade it gives and fruit it gives, birds' nests row on row.

In its green and swinging arms, mornings swing and sigh,

Roots that hug the mother earth, never let her fly.

p.d: गद्यांश: The Stepwells That Remembered the Rain
p.b:
A stepwell was never merely a place to fetch water. It was the social centre of the

village. Women descended with pitchers balanced on their heads, filled them, and exchanged news

on the way back up. Children played on the broad steps while the old rested in the shade. In this

way the stepwell stored relationships along with rainwater.

The design was carefully thought out. Wide flights of steps ran from the surface down to the

water so that however far the level fell, people could always reach it. Beside the steps lay a

deep, well-like shaft where monsoon water collected. In desert regions rain falls on only a few

days each year, so this stored water had to last twelve months.

Today many stepwells stand abandoned. Taps and pumps made the fetching of water easier, but the

groundwater has continued to fall. In several villages old stepwells are now being cleaned and

put back into use. This is not simply the preservation of old buildings. It is the return of a

water wisdom that our ancestors already possessed.

A hundred years it stands, the banyan tree,

unmoved by summer heat, unafraid of cold.

Its roots go deep, its branches reach out wide;

through every storm it stays upright and bold.

Beneath, the weary traveller rests his load,

the shepherd shelters flocks within its shade.

Children read their books beneath the leaves;

the elders told their stories where it played.

Then came the town, the road was widened out,

and talk of cutting filled the village with dread.

But the tree that gave its shade to everyone

now finds the whole village standing in its stead.

p.d: गद्यांश: The Bees That Fed the Fields
p.b:
Honeybees are counted among the hardest-working creatures on earth. A single hive holds one queen, a few males and thousands of worker bees, all of them female. The queen's only task is to lay eggs. The males never gather food. Everything else is done by the workers - building the comb, caring for the young and flying out to collect nectar from flowers.

In her whole lifetime a single bee makes only about one-twelfth of a teaspoon of honey. It therefore takes the labour of millions of bees to fill a single kilogram jar. But the bees do far more than sweeten our food. As they move from flower to flower they carry pollen with them, and this pollination is what allows much of the world's crops to set fruit. Scientists warn that if bees disappeared, most of our harvests would be in danger.

In India, beekeeping has quietly become a profitable trade. Farmers place wooden hives along the edges of their fields and gain twice over - they sell the honey, and their crops yield better because the bees have been at work. The business needs little land and little capital, which is precisely why it suits small farmers so well.

Dark clouds gathered across the sky,

and the dry earth breathed its scent.

When the first drop struck the roof,

the children pushed the window open.

The frogs began their evening song,

the peacock spread his tail and danced.

The thirsty cracks across the fields

drank deep, and smiled at last.

Rain does not bring only water -

it brings a fresh hope as well.

The land that lay so bare yesterday

is green and laughing now.

For years the village of Rampur had no library at all. The nearest one was a bus ride away in the district town, and few families could spare either the fare or the whole day.

Then a retired schoolteacher decided that if the children could not go to the library, the library would have to go to them. She fitted out an old van with wooden shelves, filled it with donated books and began driving it from village to village on a fixed weekly round. Children gathered at the village square, borrowed what they liked, and returned it the following week.

The rules were simple and unusual. There was no fine for a late book. There was no register of who owed what. And nobody was ever turned away for not having read the previous book properly. The teacher believed that fear of punishment was the quickest way to make a child stop reading.

Within a year the van was running short of books, because children were reading faster than donations arrived. Two villages asked for a second visit each week. A local shopkeeper began buying books to donate. By the third year the round had grown to eleven villages, and the teacher had trained two young helpers to drive the second van that a newspaper campaign had helped to raise money for.

What started as one woman's stubborn idea had become something the whole district now helped to run.

The old post office stands at the corner still,

its paint gone pale, its clock long stopped.

No letters wait behind the counter now,

no bell, no stamp, no queue.

Yet once a thousand hopes were folded here,

a money order sent to someone far away,

a telegram read twice before the door,

good news, and news that broke.

The world moved on to screens and silent taps,

and left the building standing in the sun.

But walk inside and you can almost hear

the rubber stamp come down.

p.d: गद्यांश: The Post Office: An Old Friend
p.b:
There was a time when a letter was the only way to reach a loved one living far away. The post office was the most important place in the village. Every morning the postman set out with a bundle of letters and walked from house to house. People waited for him, hoping that a letter had arrived for their family.

Writing a letter was an art. Choosing the paper, dipping the pen in ink, writing neatly, folding it into an envelope and sticking the stamp - every step demanded care. A reply could take weeks to arrive, so every word was chosen thoughtfully. When a letter came, the whole family gathered around it and read it again and again.

Today mobile phones and the internet have almost erased that distance. A message arrives in a moment and a reply comes back just as fast. Many post offices no longer see crowds of letters.

And yet the post office is not useless. Government documents, examination forms, bank accounts and the small savings of villages are still handled by it. Where the internet has not reached, the post office remains the only trusted link. The technology has changed, but the responsibility of reaching people remains the same.

The banyan standing at the crossroads,

a witness of a hundred years.

Its roots went deep into the ground,

its branches climbed where clouds are found.

In summer heat it offered shade,

and weary travellers were laid.

The birds have built their nests in it,

the children made their rest in it.

When rain came down it held the water,

when storms came hard it stood still firmer.

Cut it down and it stays mute -

yet the village breathes through this old root.

Now the road must widen here,

a new building must appear.

But ask this question, friend, once more -

where will you find that shade before?

p.d: गद्यांश: The Train That Came Once a Day
p.b:
The railway line passed just outside the village, but the station was in the town, fifteen kilometres away. So when the whole family finally set out to visit Uncle's house by train, everyone had to wake at four in the morning. The luggage was loaded onto a bullock cart and they left while it was still dark.

At the station the first thing they saw was the queue for tickets. Father bought the tickets and Mother gathered all the luggage in one place. People were hurrying in every direction on the platform. Some carried bundles on their heads, some carried children on their shoulders. The tea seller's voice rang out again and again - 'Chai garam, chai garam!'

When the train arrived it looked enormously long. Getting into the compartment was not easy, because of the crowd. Somehow they all got inside and found seats. Getting a seat by the window was a great thing, because fields, rivers and small stations would be visible all the way.

When the train moved there was first a jerk, and then the speed grew slowly. The fields slipped behind and the birds sitting on the wires flew away. By the time they reached Uncle's town it was evening. The day was very tiring, but the world seen through the train window felt completely new.
